newsitem.title: GERMANY: Stainless production shifts may impact on nickel.
newsitem.headline: Stainless production shifts may impact on nickel.

text.p: A shift in the production of stainless steel to emerging nations means suppliers of raw materials will have to follow their customers, analyst Markus Moll of Austria's SMR consultancy told an industry conference.
The stainless steel industry accounts for two thirds of global nickel consumption and also consumes chrome, nickel-bearing scrap and molybdenum.
"Raw materials suppliers have to look for partnerships in new centres of consumption," Moll said in response to questions at the Metal Bulletin stainless steel conference.
"Traditional stainless steel makers should be quicker in establishing joint ventures, they are too much in a waiting position," he also said.
Moll said suppliers needed to adjust to changing demands from their industrial partners -- the size of plants often did not match that in traditional stainless steel industries in the western world.
There was also competition from local raw materials, such as domestic chrome and manganese in India's low-nickel stainless grades.
Moll's speech focused on stainless steel long products, such as billets, bars, wire rod and tubes.
At 2.5 million tonnes of annual production, they roughly equal one fifth of total stainless output.
Import growth in 1985-95 of those products in seven key countries was nine percent per annum.
But a slump in 1996 imports reduced the annual growth rate in the (1985-96) 11-year period to just five percent.
With this pattern likely to continue, the main loser would be Japan while Europe should continue to supply its traditional markets in North America.
The seven countries were China, South Korea, Taiwan, India, Brazil, South Africa and Australia.
They might add a combined one million tonnes of new capacity to world supply of long products by 2005, turning into net exporters by 1999.
